title: Nachiketa at Death's door
hook: a boy waits three days at Death's house and asks what happens after

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gita's worn clothes. Your line was garb of flesh. A new week now, and a boy who goes to Death's own house.

To whom will you give me? A boy asks his father that in the middle of a great sacrifice, where the father is giving away what he owns, including cows too old to give milk. The boy asks a second time. Then a third. And the father, losing patience, snaps: to Death I give you. That's how the Katha Upanishad, a Hindu scripture, begins. And the boy, Nachiketa, goes.
screen: `TO WHOM WILL YOU GIVE ME?` → `TO DEATH I GIVE YOU.` → `AND THE BOY GOES.`

segments.voice: First, the waiting. Nachiketa reaches the house of Yama, lord of death, and Yama is away. The boy waits three nights without food. When Yama comes home he is troubled, because a guest has gone unfed in his house, and he offers three wishes, one for each night. Second, the question. Nachiketa spends his first wish on his father, that he'll be calm and glad to see him again. The second is to learn a sacred fire. The third is the question itself: when someone dies, some say they still are, and some say they are not. Teach me which. Third, the refusal. Yama tries to wriggle out of it. Even the gods have doubted about this, he says; it's subtle; ask for something else. He lays out the alternatives: sons and grandsons, cattle and gold, horses, land, a long life, chariots and music. Nachiketa turns them all down. These things wear out, he says. Keep your horses, keep your songs. I want the answer. Fourth, the good and the pleasant. Only now does Yama begin to teach. Two things come to a person, he says: the good and the pleasant. The wise choose the good. What follows is his teaching on the self that is not born and does not die. Hindus read this Upanishad as scripture, and teachers keep coming back to Nachiketa: a boy at Death's door who would rather have a true answer than everything Death can give him.
screen: `THREE NIGHTS AT DEATH'S HOUSE.` · `DO THEY STILL EXIST, OR NOT?` · `CHARIOTS AND GOLD, REFUSED.` · `THE GOOD OVER THE PLEASANT.` · then, large: `NACHIKETA'S QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Let your biggest question come up, not the one you'd put on a form but the one underneath: about death, or a person, or what any of this is for. Say it to yourself in one plain sentence, and don't try to answer it. Just hold it, the way Nachiketa held his through three hungry nights, and if other thoughts crowd in, come back to the sentence.
Nachiketa, the boy in the Katha Upanishad who waits at Yama's house and asks what happens after death. Today's word.
Your line: Nachiketa's question. He wanted the answer more than the horses. Day seven hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Hindus study the Katha Upanishad as scripture, often with a teacher, and the story of Nachiketa is told to children and adults as a teaching on courage, truth and the self.
